title: Hermits on Carmel (c. 1200)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day with the Jesuits: a morning offering, God at the sink, the examen at night. Your line was god in all things. Where did it turn up when you looked back last night? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

A long green ridge runs down to the sea on the coast of the Holy Land, and at its top a man is crouched on the ground, his face pressed between his knees. He has just come through a very public day: a crowd, an altar, fire from heaven. Now he has climbed away from all of it to pray alone, while his servant keeps going to look out at the sea. The man is the prophet Elijah, Elias in the Douay-Rheims, and the ridge is Mount Carmel. Long after, a small group of hermits would come to live on that same mountain. Today we begin a new school of prayer, and it takes its name from the place.
screen: `A RIDGE ABOVE THE SEA.` → `A PROPHET, FACE TO HIS KNEES.` → `HERMITS ON THE SAME MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Carmelite. Someone who belongs to Carmel, to the order that grew up on that mountain. Start with Elijah, because the hermits did. In the third book of Kings, as the Douay-Rheims names it, Elijah stands on Carmel and calls a wavering people to choose the Lord. Fire falls on his offering. Then, the text says, he goes up to the top of Carmel, bows to the ground, and "put his face between his knees." He prays, and he keeps praying, and his servant keeps going back to watch the sea, until at last a little cloud rises out of the sea, small as a man's foot, and the drought breaks in rain. That's the picture the hermits treasured. Not the fire. The man alone on the mountaintop, praying low and waiting. Much later, tradition says, a small group of Western Christians, pilgrims and penitents from Europe, settled on Carmel as hermits. They lived in caves and small cells on the slope, near a spring that tradition linked to Elijah, and they prayed. They looked to Elijah as their model, and in time they also dedicated their life to Mary, and tradition says they built a little chapel in her honor. That double inheritance is still in the order's full name: the Brothers of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel. Later the Carmelites would spread far from the mountain, and saints would come from Spain and France and elsewhere. But it begins small: a few people, a ridge, a spring, and a prophet's posture of waiting prayer. Carmel is a reminder that prayer can start as simply as going somewhere quiet and staying low.
screen: `ELIJAH ON CARMEL.` · `FACE BETWEEN HIS KNEES, WAITING.` · `HERMITS NEAR A SPRING.` · `ELIJAH AND MARY: A DOUBLE INHERITANCE.` · then, large: `A LITTLE CLOUD, LIKE A MAN'S FOOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a hermit's corner. Look around wherever you are for the quietest small spot within reach: the end of a sofa, the floor beside the bed, a step outside, even a parked car. Go there if you can. Sit low and lean forward a little, the way Elijah did. Settle, and breathe. Don't ask for fire. Just wait, the way his servant watched the sea. If you pray, you can pray without words, or with one line of a psalm. If you don't, rest in the quiet of your corner. The bell holds the time.
Carmelite. One who belongs to Carmel: the order that began with hermits on Elijah's mountain and gave its life to Mary. Today's word.
Your line: elijah's mountain. Today, go back to your hermit's corner once more, even for a minute, and wait there without asking for anything. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Carmelite friars, nuns and lay Carmelites look to Elijah and to Mary as models, and give a central place in their lives to silent, personal prayer.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of 3 Kings 18:42 to confirm (only 'put his face between his knees' is quoted). The servant's repeated looking (the text says seven times) and the cloud 'like a man's foot' (Douay 3 Kings 18:44; KJV has 'hand') are paraphrased; confirm.

The hermits as Western (Latin) pilgrims and penitents, living near the 'spring of Elijah', and building a chapel to Mary: drawn from Carmelite tradition and the Rule's address; hedged where possible. Confirm.
Full name now given as 'Brothers of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel' (Latin Beatissimae): confirm wording.
'Saints would come from Spain and France' looks ahead to Teresa, John of the Cross and Thérèse later in this section; confirm acceptable.
The date in the title (c. 1200) is from the index; the voice states no date.
